author: AI Editorial Team (Esi)
key_learning_objective: Identify incorrect self-care teaching for a client on lisinopril.
question_stem: A client with heart failure is prescribed lisinopril. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.A: "A dry, nagging cough can be a side effect of this medication."
options.B: "I will use a salt substitute to lower my sodium intake."
options.C: "I will change positions slowly to avoid dizziness."
options.D: "I will report any swelling of my lips or tongue right away."

rationales.A: Correct understanding. A persistent dry cough is a well-known ACE inhibitor side effect.
rationales.B: Needs teaching (correct answer). Salt substitutes are high in potassium; combined with an ACE inhibitor they raise the risk of hyperkalemia and should be avoided.
rationales.C: Correct understanding. ACE inhibitors can cause orthostatic hypotension; slow position changes are appropriate.
rationales.D: Correct understanding. Lip/tongue swelling suggests angioedema, a medical emergency that must be reported immediately.

key_takeaway: ACE inhibitors raise potassium - avoid salt substitutes. Watch for cough and angioedema.
nclex_test_taking_tip: On 'needs further teaching' items, hunt for the one wrong/unsafe statement.
memory_trick: ACE = raises potassium; salt substitutes ARE potassium - a bad mix.
clinical_pearls: Angioedema is life-threatening - stop the drug and get help.
ACE cough is dry and non-productive; may prompt a switch to an ARB.
